title: Ratios, Rates, and Percentages
lead: Part 1 of Problem-Solving and Data Analysis: ratios, proportions, unit rates and percentages. The domain rewards organization more than algebra, and this material is mostly arithmetic with structure. The multiplier idea here is the same one behind the exponential models in Class 12.

parts.title: Part 1 · Three words to keep apart
parts.html:
WordWhat it isExample
RatioA comparison of two quantities. It can be written three ways: a to b, a:b, or a/b.A shelf holds 6 novels and 4 atlases. The ratio of novels to atlases is 6 to 4, 6:4, or 6/4.
ProportionA statement that two ratios are equal.6/4 = 15/10
RateA ratio whose two quantities have different units, worked out as a division.A pump moves 84 litres in 4 minutes: 84 ÷ 4 = 21 litres per minute.

Order matters. “Novels to atlases” is 6:4. “Atlases to novels” is 4:6. The ratio follows the order of the words, and a wrong choice often has the right numbers in the wrong order.

Equivalent ratios. Multiplying or dividing both numbers by the same amount gives the same ratio: 6:4 = 3:2 = 30:20. Reduce a ratio the way a fraction is reduced.

parts.title: Part 2 · Part to part, part to whole
parts.html:
A ratio can compare one part with another part, or one part with the whole. A question often gives one kind and asks for the other, so name which kind each ratio is before using it.

Example. A trail mix is made of nuts and raisins only. The ratio of nuts to trail mix is 3 to 8. What is the ratio of nuts to raisins? 3 to 8 is part to whole: 3 parts nuts in every 8 parts of mix
Raisins are the rest of the whole: 8−3=5 parts
Raisins to trail mix is 5 to 8 (part to whole)
Nuts to raisins is 3 to 5 (part to part) → 3:5

Going the other way, add the parts to get the whole: nuts to raisins of 3:5 means 3 + 5 = 8 parts in total, so nuts are 3/8 of the mix.

Ratios with totals. “The ratio of cats to dogs is 3:2 and there are 40 animals in total.” Total parts = 3 + 2 = 5, so one part = 8. Cats = 24, dogs = 16. The parts method is faster than algebra.

Common mistake. Treating a part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole. A ratio of 3:2 does not mean the first quantity is 3/2 of the total or 3/2 of anything except the second quantity. Its share of the total is 3/5.

parts.title: Part 3 · Solving with a proportion
parts.html:
When two quantities grow together at a constant ratio, one known pair and half of a second pair are enough to find the missing value.

  1. Write an equation with two equal ratios, in words first.
  2. Put in the known values and a variable for the unknown.
  3. Solve, usually by cross-multiplying.
Example. 5 notebooks cost $8. At the same price, how much do 20 notebooks cost? notebooks / dollars = notebooks / dollars
58=20x
5x=160 → x=32 → $32

Two correct set-ups. There is more than one right way to arrange a proportion. Either rule below works.

RuleSet-upResult
Same unit across each row: notebooks on top, dollars underneath5 / 8 = 20 / xx = 32
Same unit inside each fraction: notebooks on one side, dollars on the other5 / 20 = 8 / xx = 32
Wrong: matching units sit diagonally5 / 8 = x / 20x = 12.5, which is not the cost

Writing the units beside each number makes the diagonal error visible before any arithmetic is done. A quick sense check also catches it: 20 notebooks cannot cost less than four times the price of 5.

Direct or inverse? Decide the direction before setting anything up.

DirectionSet-up
Same direction: more of one means more of the othera/b = c/d, then cross-multiply
Opposite direction: more of one means less of the otherThe product stays constant
5 machines take 7 hours. How long do 7 machines take? More machines, less time → inverse → machines × hours is constant
5×7=35 → 357=5 hours

Mislabelling the direction is the main error here.

parts.title: Part 4 · Rates and unit rates
parts.html:
A unit rate is the amount for one unit of the second quantity: per hour, per item, per litre. Once the unit rate is known, any other amount is one multiplication away.

RateFormulaRearranged
Speeddistance ÷ timedistance = speed × time
Unit pricetotal price ÷ number of unitstotal price = unit price × number of units
Example. A cyclist rides 54 km in 3 hours at a constant speed. How far does the cyclist ride in 5 hours? Unit rate: 54÷3=18 km per hour
Apply it: 18×5=90 → 90 km

The same question can be solved as a proportion, 54/3 = x/5. Finding the unit rate first is usually quicker when the question asks for more than one amount.

Unit rates. “12 ounces cost $3.60. What is the price per pound?” 3.60 / 12 = $0.30 per ounce, then 0.30 × 16 = $4.80 per pound. Going from per-ounce to per-pound means multiplying by 16, and the SAT sets its trap at exactly this step.

Common mistake. Unit errors in compound rates. To turn 90 km per hour into a per-second rate, dividing by 60 once is not enough: hours → minutes → seconds is two divisions, and a missing factor changes the answer by 60. Write the units as fractions and cancel them like numbers: km/h × h/min × min/s. Hours cancel, minutes cancel, and 90 ÷ 3600 = 0.025 km per second, or 25 metres per second.

parts.title: Part 5 · Percentages: part, whole, percent
parts.html:
A percentage is a ratio out of 100 that compares a part with a whole. “Percent” means “per hundred”.

percent = (part ÷ whole) × 100

There are three quantities here: the part, the whole and the percent. Any two of them give the third.

Example. A student answers 18 of 40 questions correctly. What percent is that? part =18, whole =40
18÷40=0.45 → 0.45×100=45 → 45%
The three percentage questionsCompute
What is p% of n?(p / 100) × n
What percent is a of b?(a / b) × 100
a is p% of what?a ÷ (p / 100)

Watch the labels. The part is not always the smaller number. 140% of 15 is 1.40 × 15 = 21, and here the “part” is larger than the “whole”. The whole is whatever follows the word “of”.

Percentages that complete each other. All the parts of a whole add up to 100%, so a missing part can be found by subtraction first.

Example. A school has 60 teachers. 35% of them teach science, and the rest teach other subjects. How many teach other subjects? Other subjects: 100%−35%=65%
0.65×60=39 → 39 teachers

The same idea fills a gap in a table: if three of four categories are 18%, 27% and 31%, the fourth is 100 − 18 − 27 − 31 = 24%.

Equivalent forms. A percentage can be written as a ratio, a fraction or a decimal. Use whichever is easiest for the calculation.

PercentRatioFractionDecimal
40%40:100 = 2:540/100 = 2/50.4
75%75:100 = 3:475/100 = 3/40.75
125%125:100 = 5:4125/100 = 5/41.25

To turn a percent into a decimal, drop the % sign and move the decimal point two places to the left: 35% → 0.35, 6% → 0.06, 112% → 1.12. The decimal is the form to calculate with: 35% of 280 is 0.35 × 280 = 98.

Translating the words. A percentage sentence can be turned into an equation word by word.

WordWrite
whatx
is=
of×
percent÷ 100
Example. 27 is what percent of 45? 27=(x100)×45
x=27×100÷45=60 → 60%

parts.title: Part 6 · Percent change and the multiplier method
parts.html:
Percent change measures a change against the value it started from.

  1. Find the difference between the initial and final values.
  2. Divide the difference by the initial value.
  3. Multiply by 100.

percent change = (difference ÷ initial) × 100

Example. The price of a monthly bus pass rises from $80 to $92. What is the percent increase? Difference: 92−80=12
12÷80=0.15 → 0.15×100=15 → 15% increase

The denominator is always the original value, never the new one. Dividing by 92 here gives about 13%, which is a common wrong choice.

Percent change also has three quantities: the initial value, the final value and the percent change. Any two give the third, and the multiplier below is the quickest way to move between them.

Every percentage question runs through one idea: a percent change is multiplication by a factor.

  • Increase by 15% → multiply by 1.15
  • Decrease by 15% → multiply by 0.85
  • Successive changes multiply: +10% then −10% is 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, a net 1% decrease. Consecutive percent changes do not add.
Finding the initial value. A coat costs $63 after a 30% discount. What was the price before the discount? After a 30% discount the price is 100%−30%=70% of the original
0.70x=63 → x=63÷0.70=90 → $90
Example. A $240 jacket is discounted 25%, then a 10% tax is applied to the discounted price. What is the final price? 240×0.75=180
180×1.10=198 → $198

Percent greater than, percent less than. “A is 50% more than B” means A = 1.5B. “A is 40% less than B” means A = 0.6B. The trap: the relation is not symmetric. If A is 25% less than B, then A = 0.75B, so B = A / 0.75 ≈ 1.333A, which is 33⅓% more than A. “A is 25% less than B” does not mean “B is 25% more than A”. Write both in terms of one variable and compare.

Reverse percentage. After a 20% discount and a 6% tax, the final price was $127.20. What was the original price? original ×0.80×1.06=127.20
original =127.200.80×1.06=127.200.848=150 → $150

Do not combine the percents by adding or subtracting. A 20% discount and a 6% tax are not a 14% discount. Multiplying the factors is the only correct chain.

parts.title: Part 7 · The Desmos angle
parts.html:
• Percent chains are one line: type 240 × 0.75 × 1.10.
  • Reverse percentage: compute 127.20 / (0.8 × 1.06) directly, or graph y = x × 0.8 × 1.06 and y = 127.20 and read the intersection.
  • Proportions are faster by cross-multiplication than in Desmos.
  • Unit conversions with awkward factors (such as 3.785 L per gallon): multiply through the conversion factors in one line.

parts.title: Part 8 · Things to remember
parts.html:
• A ratio follows the order of the words in the question.
  • Label each ratio as part to part or part to whole. Parts add up to the whole.
  • In a proportion, matching units go in the same row or in the same fraction, never diagonally.
  • Decide whether the quantities move in the same direction or in opposite directions before setting up.
  • Unit rate = amount ÷ number of units. Speed = distance ÷ time. Unit price = total price ÷ units.
  • Percent means per hundred: p% = p/100. To get the decimal, drop the % sign and move the decimal point two places left.
  • In a percentage sentence, “what” is x, “is” is =, “of” is ×, and “percent” is ÷ 100.
  • Percent = part ÷ whole × 100. The whole follows the word “of”, and all parts add up to 100%.
  • Percent change = difference ÷ initial value × 100. Always divide by the initial value.
  • A percent change is multiplication by a factor, and successive changes multiply.

parts.title: Part 9 · Rates, ratios and mixtures: harder cases
parts.html:
Converting square and cubic units. A conversion factor for length must be used twice for an area and three times for a volume.

A floor has an area of 54 square feet. What is its area in square yards? (1 yard = 3 feet) 1 square yard =3×3=9 square feet
54÷9=6 square yards
Dividing by 3 only once gives 18, which will be among the choices.

Average rate of change is the change in the quantity divided by the change in time (or in whatever the input is). It is the slope between two points.

A tank holds 500 litres after 3 hours and 140 litres after 9 hours. What is the average rate of change? 140−5009−3=−3606=−60 → the tank loses 60 litres per hour

Average speed is total distance over total time. It is not the average of the two speeds.

A driver covers 120 km at 60 km/h and then 120 km at 40 km/h. What is the average speed for the trip? Times: 120÷60=2 hours and 120÷40=3 hours
Total: 240 km in 5 hours → 240 ÷ 5 = 48 km/h
The average of 60 and 40 is 50, which is the trap.

Three-part ratios. When two ratios share a quantity, scale them until the shared quantity has the same number in both.

The ratio of A to B is 2:3 and the ratio of B to C is 6:5. If A, B and C total 150, what is C? B is 3 in one ratio and 6 in the other → double the first, so A : B = 4 : 6
Combined → A : B : C = 4 : 6 : 5 → 15 parts
C is 5 of the 15 parts → 5/15 × 150 = 50

Mixtures. Track the amount of the pure substance and the total amount separately. The total changes when you add to it.

A tank holds 40 litres of a 10% acid solution. How many litres of a 60% acid solution must be added to make a 20% solution? Acid now: 0.10×40=4 litres
Add x litres → acid 4+0.60x, total 40+x
4+0.60x40+x=0.20
4+0.60x=8+0.20x → 0.40x=4 → x=10 litres
Check: 10 litres of acid in 50 litres is 20%.

Common mistake. Aiming for 20% of the original 40 litres (8 litres of acid) and adding just enough to reach it. The total is no longer 40 once you pour more in.
